title: Getting dressed, washing up: the hitpa'el
why: The first new binyan of the unit: the hitpa'el, the verb pattern for actions "turned back on yourself" (getting dressed, washing, getting married). After the pi'el in unit 9, you describe your morning routine in the present and the past.

{"lessons": ["

The hitpa'el: the verb turned back on yourself

In English, you \"get dressed,\" \"wash up,\" \"get married,\" or you add a word like myself: \"I dress myself.\" Hebrew needs none of that: it's the shape of the verb, the hitpa'el binyan, that tells you the action comes back to the person doing it.

אֲנִי מִתְלַבֵּשׁ.I'm getting dressed. [ani mitlabesh]

In the present, the hitpa'el is easy to spot: it starts with מִתְ־ (mit), followed by the three letters of the root, with a then e: מִתְ + לבשׁ → מִתְלַבֵּשׁ. You already know one verb from this binyan: מִתְכַּוֵּן (mitkaven, to intend).

FormHebrewPronunciation
m. sg.מִתְלַבֵּשׁmitlabesh
f. sg.מִתְלַבֶּשֶׁתmitlabeshet
m. pl.מִתְלַבְּשִׁיםmitlabshim
f. pl.מִתְלַבְּשׁוֹתmitlabshot

The trap for English speakers: looking for a word for \"myself, yourself, herself.\" No need! הִיא מִתְלַבֶּשֶׁת simply means \"she's getting dressed.\"

", "

In the past and the infinitive

In the past, מִתְ־ becomes הִתְ־ (hit), and you add the same person endings as for כָּתַבְתִּי:

PronounPastPronunciation
אֲנִיהִתְלַבַּשְׁתִּיhitlabashti
אַתָּההִתְלַבַּשְׁתָּhitlabashta
אַתְּהִתְלַבַּשְׁתְּhitlabasht
הוּאהִתְלַבֵּשׁhitlabesh
הִיאהִתְלַבְּשָׁהhitlabsha
אֲנַחְנוּהִתְלַבַּשְׁנוּhitlabashnu
אַתֶּםהִתְלַבַּשְׁתֶּםhitlabashtem
הֵם / הֵןהִתְלַבְּשׁוּhitlabshu

The infinitive starts with לְהִתְ־: לְהִתְלַבֵּשׁ (lehitlabesh), לְהִתְקַלֵּחַ (lehitkaleakh). It follows the verbs you already know:

אֲנִי צָרִיךְ לְהִתְלַבֵּשׁ.I have to get dressed. [ani tsarikh lehitlabesh]

The letter ח doesn't like e: when it ends the root, the feminine takes a. הוּא מִתְקַלֵּחַ (mitkaleakh), but הִיא מִתְקַלַּחַת (mitkalakhat).

", "

My morning routine

בַּבֹּקֶר אֲנִי קָם, מִתְקַלֵּחַ וּמִתְלַבֵּשׁ.In the morning, I get up, shower and get dressed. [ba-boker ani kam, mitkaleakh u-mitlabesh]
אַחֲרֵי הַמִּקְלַחַת הוּא מִתְגַּלֵּחַ.After the shower, he shaves. [akharei ha-miklakhat hu mitgaleakh]
הִיא מִתְאַרְגֶּנֶת מַהֵר.She gets ready quickly. [hi mit'argenet maher]

Two verbs take a preposition, just like in English: מִתְעַנְיֵן בְּ־ (to be interested in) and מִתְחַתֵּן עִם (to marry, to get married to). Note that Hebrew says \"marry with\" someone.

נֹעָה מִתְעַנְיֶנֶת בְּמוּזִיקָה.Noa is interested in music. [No'a mit'anyenet be-muzika]
דָּנָה מִתְחַתֶּנֶת עִם רוֹן.Dana is marrying Ron. [Dana mitkhatenet im Ron]

When the root starts with ס or שׁ, the ת moves after that letter: מִסְתַּכֵּל (mistakel, he looks). With צ, it moves after it and even turns into ט: מִצְטַלֵּם (mitstalem, he gets his picture taken). You'll recognize them easily.
